slides.title: What math you actually need for ML research
slides.body:
Reading ML papers requires a specific mathematical vocabulary. Not all of math — a focused subset that shows up in nearly every paper.

- **Linear algebra**: vectors, matrices, dot products, norms, eigendecomposition. The shape language of ML.
- **Calculus**: derivatives, gradients, chain rule. The mechanics of training.
- **Probability**: random variables, expectations, distributions, Bayes' rule. The model of uncertainty.
- **Statistics**: estimation, MLE, hypothesis testing. How we turn data into claims.
- **Information theory**: entropy, KL divergence, mutual information. The vocabulary of ML losses.

This lesson is a tour. Each topic gets one slide of essentials — enough to know what you're missing if a paper assumes it. Each links out to a deeper foundations page.

slides.title: Linear algebra essentials
slides.body:
The four operations you'll see constantly:

**Matrix-vector product** `Wx`. Linear combination of W's columns weighted by x.

**Matrix-matrix product** `AB`. Each entry `(AB)[i,j] = Σ_k A[i,k] · B[k,j]`. Order matters: `AB ≠ BA` in general.

**Dot product** `x · y = Σ x_i y_i`. Measures how 'aligned' two vectors are. Equals `|x| |y| cos(θ)`. The dot product *is* what attention computes when comparing queries to keys.

**Norm** `||x||`. The most common is L2: `||x||_2 = √(Σ x_i²)`. L1 is `Σ |x_i|`. Norms quantify 'size' of a vector.

Two decompositions worth knowing by name:

- **Eigendecomposition** `A = QΛQ^(-1)`. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues. The eigenbasis is where A looks like a scaling.
- **Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)** `A = UΣV^T`. Generalizes eigendecomposition to non-square matrices. Underlies LoRA, PCA, and many dimension-reduction methods.

If you can compute matrix shapes by hand and know what 'rank' means, you can read most ML papers. See [[linear-algebra-foundations]].

question.question: If A is [m×n] and B is [n×p], what's the shape of AB?
options: Undefined — only square matrices can multiply
question.explanation: Matrix multiplication chains the inner dimensions. A is [m×n], B is [n×p]; the n's cancel; result is [m×p]. This is the most-used shape rule in ML — knowing it cold lets you sanity-check architecture diagrams in seconds.

slides.title: Calculus + chain rule
slides.body:
ML training is calculus on weights. The model defines a loss as a function of weights `L(W)`; you compute the gradient `∂L/∂W`; you take a step in the direction of negative gradient.

The **chain rule** is the engine:

$$\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$$

Applied to deep networks, chain rule is what propagates gradients backward through every layer. Get the chain rule wrong and your gradients are wrong. (See [[backpropagation]].)

Multivariable extension: the gradient of a scalar function of a vector is a vector of partial derivatives:

$$\nabla_x f(x) = \left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}, \ldots\right]$$

Gradient descent: `W ← W - η · ∇_W L`.

The **Hessian** is the matrix of second derivatives. It tells you about local curvature. Most modern optimizers (Adam, etc.) approximate Hessian information without computing it explicitly. See [[calculus-foundations]] and [[optimization-theory]].

slides.title: Probability + statistics
slides.body:
**Random variables, expectations, variance**: the basic vocabulary. `E[X]` is what you'd get on average; `Var[X]` is how spread out it is.

**Distributions you'll see constantly**:

- Bernoulli (coin flip)
- Categorical (one-of-K)
- Normal / Gaussian — appears everywhere because of the central limit theorem
- Multinomial — sample from K classes

**Conditional probability** `P(A|B)` is the basis of Bayes' rule:

$$P(A|B) = \frac{P(B|A) \cdot P(A)}{P(B)}$$

Flipping conditioning. **Critical**: `P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A)` in general. The base-rate fallacy is exactly the confusion between these.

**Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)**: given data, find parameters that make the data most probable under the model. Cross-entropy loss minimization is MLE. (See [[statistics-foundations]] and [[probability-foundations]].)

slides.title: Information theory
slides.body:
**Entropy** `H(X) = -Σ p(x) log p(x)`. The expected number of bits needed to encode X. High entropy means the distribution is spread out (uncertain); low entropy means it's concentrated.

**KL divergence** `KL(P || Q) = Σ p(x) log(p(x) / q(x))`. Measures how 'different' two distributions are. Asymmetric: `KL(P||Q) ≠ KL(Q||P)`. Used in RLHF, VAEs, and basically everywhere distributions are compared.

**Cross-entropy** `H(P, Q) = -Σ p(x) log q(x)`. The standard ML loss. Also asymmetric. The next-token-prediction loss is cross-entropy between the true distribution (one-hot for the actual next token) and the model's predicted distribution.

**Mutual information** `I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y)`. How much knowing Y reduces uncertainty about X. Foundation of representation learning objectives.

If you only learn one of these deeply: **KL divergence**. It shows up in policy regularization (RLHF), generative modeling, and information bottleneck arguments throughout ML. See [[information-theory]].

question.question: Why is cross-entropy loss the standard objective for next-token prediction?
options: It's equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation: minimizing cross-entropy = maximizing the likelihood that the model assigns to the actual training data
question.explanation: Cross-entropy is `-Σ p_true(x) log p_model(x)`. With p_true being one-hot (the actual next token), this becomes `-log p_model(actual_token)`, which is exactly the negative log-likelihood. Minimizing cross-entropy IS maximum likelihood estimation. This is one of the most important conceptual unifications in ML.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
These five areas are the math substrate for ML research. The rest of the AI Researcher path builds on them:

- [[info-theory-basics]] — entropy, KL, mutual information at applied depth
- [[statistics-for-ml]] — estimation, hypothesis testing, calibration
- [[transformer-deep-dive]] — the architecture, with these tools
- [[training-dynamics]] — what loss curves and gradient norms mean

Key takeaways:
- Linear algebra: dot products, matrix shapes, eigendecomposition / SVD
- Calculus: chain rule, gradients, gradient descent
- Probability: Bayes, expectation, common distributions
- Statistics: MLE, hypothesis testing
- Information theory: entropy, KL, cross-entropy

If any of these feels rusty, the foundations pages have full lessons. If they all feel familiar, you're ready for the rest of the path.
